analysis.one_liner: Makes community college tuition-free for everyone and public four-year college tuition-free for working- and middle-class students.
analysis.headline: A tuition-free college bill backed by 49 House Democrats never got a hearing or a vote in the Republican-led committee, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1880 would have used federal grants to states to eliminate tuition and required fees for every student at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for working-class and middle-class students at public four-year colleges. It also would have paid for extra student support services and sent any surplus revenue from the federal student loan program into Pell Grants, which help the lowest-income students. It applied for fiscal years 2019 through 2027. Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced it in April 2017 with 49 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support. It was sent to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and the bill expired with the Congress in January 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges — who would owe no tuition or required fees at all — and working-class and middle-class students at public four-year colleges, who would get the same break. Low-income students would also benefit from the Pell Grant top-up, since any money the federal loan program brings in beyond its costs would fund Pell awards instead of sitting in the Treasury. Public colleges would gain a guaranteed federal funding stream for FY2019-2027.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a federal grant program to eliminate tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges and universities.
Extends the same tuition elimination to working-class and middle-class students at public four-year institutions of higher education.
Funds student support services — such as academic guidance — alongside the tuition grants, for fiscal years 2019 through 2027.
Directs the Department of Education to use any excess revenue generated by the Federal Direct Loan program to carry out the Federal Pell Grant program, which aids the lowest-income students.
Sets the grants to run for each of fiscal years 2019 through 2027.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the grants for nine fiscal years. The bill funds part of the cost by redirecting surplus revenue from the federal Direct Loan program into Pell Grants, so any program receiving that revenue, or any spending competing for it, would bear part of the cost. Private nonprofit colleges are left out of the tuition grants and would face a relative disadvantage against tuition-free public options.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; private colleges lose out

drawbacks.text: The bill commits federal funding for fiscal years 2019 through 2027 — a nine-year spending commitment with a real cost to taxpayers, paid for in part by redirecting surplus revenue from the federal Direct Loan program, money that would otherwise flow to the Treasury for other purposes.
The tuition grants apply only to public institutions of higher education, so private colleges and their students are excluded and tuition-free public colleges would draw enrollment away from them.

A good-faith objection to free-tuition designs generally is that some of the benefit goes to students who could pay, since anyone who meets the income definition at a covered public school pays nothing — the bill caps this by limiting four-year coverage to working- and middle-class students, but community college coverage is universal with no income test.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a college education with no tuition bill for community college students and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year schools — is large and reaches millions of households directly. The cost is a nine-year federal spending commitment, partially funded by redirecting loan-program surplus rather than new taxes, which shifts some burden onto other priorities. The design limits four-year coverage to working- and middle-class students, which keeps the cost lower than universal coverage, but community college coverage has no income test. Whether the trade is worth it is a legitimate policy judgment; the strongest design criticism is that a federal free-tuition mandate could reshape how states and colleges set tuition over the long run.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the College for All Act of 2017 on April 4, 2017.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
Forty-nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The full action history shows only the introduction and the referral — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo. Because the bill never came to a vote, students continue paying tuition at community and public colleges, and the House majority never had to take a recorded position on the program. The committee chair who declined to act and the members who preferred no vote on the question came out ahead; the bill's cosponsors gained a public record of support without a roll call.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the House majority avoided a vote

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to eliminate tuition at community colleges and at public four-year colleges for working- and middle-class students.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-NC, chair)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: Public community colleges, two-year tribal colleges, and public four-year institutions would have received federal grants to cover tuition for their students, plus funding for student support services, through FY2027.

The tuition grants apply to public institutions of higher education, so private colleges and their students are excluded, and tuition-free public options would pull enrollment and tuition dollars away from them.

industries.industry: Federal Direct Loan program / student aid administration
industries.note: The bill would route any excess revenue the federal Direct Loan program generates into Pell Grants, redirecting surplus that currently goes to the Treasury.
